# Discussion

In this study we tested if community biomass is a general indicator of mechanisms mediating global change impacts on plant diversity. We found support for the role of biomass at the temperature and nutrient limited alpine site, but at the sub-alpine site it worked less well. At the sub-alpine site, warming and nitrogen addition affected diversity directly instead of indirectly through community biomass. By including environmental affinities, specifically for light and reaction, we were able to explain the underlying mechanisms of community responses to global change. 
<!-- The last sentence might need some modification -->

### Community biomass mediates global change impacts on diversity in alpine sites

Our main hypothesis was that the three global change drivers, warming, nitrogen addition, and clipping, operate through increased community biomass favoring more intense competition, especially for light, resulting in a decrease in vascular plant diversity. In line with the first part of this hypothesis, we found a strong increase in community biomass with warming and nitrogen addition in both alpine and sub-alpine communities, paralleling the findings of previous studies manipulating one or both of these drivers [@elmendorf2012plot; @Humbert2016-wg; @Zhang2023-xg]. Warming can increase biomass because of higher rates of photosynthesis, a longer growing season, or because higher microbial activity can increase nutrient availability, while nitrogen addition directly increases nutrient availability. The alpine site was strongly temperature and nutrient limited, resulting in a four to five times increase of community biomass with either warming or nitrogen addition. This co-limitation at the alpine site could be an explanation for the stronger mediation through biomass compared to the sub-alpine site. <!-- Last sentence, needs more explanation -->

<!-- Needs different logic. can say that biomass decreased see other studies, but we can say it happened via this mechanism -->
Warming and nitrogen addition decreased diversity mediated through increased community biomass. Negative effects on diversity and richness have also been observed in several warming and/or nitrogen addition experiments [@klein2004experimental; @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @wu2020additive; @shangguan2024plant; @anderson2025experimental]. The diversity loss could be due to a shift towards more competitive interactions, where warming and nitrogen addition favors taller and fast growing (resource-acquisitive) species such as graminoids at the expense of resource conservative species such as many forbs [@Klanderud2005-yx; @Wang2012-cj; @Fu2016-dw]. Warming and nitrogen addition indirectly decreased diversity and evenness, but not richness (Supplement Figure S5), suggesting a shift in abundance of species with different competitive abilities, rather than the loss of species.

While the effects of nitrogen addition and clipping were only indirectly, warming also directly increased Shannon diversity, at low levels of nitrogen addition (\< 25 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^). An increase in diversity in response to warming is less common in warming experiments [@dainese2024global], but often observed over larger areas in historical observations [@steinbauer2018accelerated]. One alternative explanation for this direct warming effect could be species turnover through colonization or extinction unrelated to competitive interactions. Warming shifted the environmental affinities of the alpine community towards more shade tolerant, warmer and nutrient demanding species, supporting this idea. Since warming increased both species richness and evenness in the alpine community, this suggests that such species both colonized these communities and increased in abundance. Colonization is likely a more common mechanisms than extinctions, because it generally happen faster than extinctions and there is often an extinction lag in alpine communities [@Vandvik2020-hu; @Alexander2015-gu; @block2022ecological].

### Alternative mechanisms drive diversity shifts in the sub-alpine

The sub-alpine site was less temperature and nutrient limited compared to the alpine site and also had fewer species to begin with, which could partly explain why we found much weaker indirect effects of the global change drivers via community biomass on diversity. Warming and nitrogen addition had less impacted on community biomass (i.e. lower explanatory power in the regression model; @fig-1-biomass-diversity a), yielding a smaller range of biomass to manipulate.

Instead, we found stronger and negative direct effects of warming and nitrogen addition on diversit in the sub-alpine site. Warming also directly decreased species richness, while nitrogen addition decreased evenness, suggesting a loss of species due to warming, while nitrogen addition caused a shift in species abundance. Using a similar SEM approach to study direct and indirect drivers of plant diversity in three temperate grasslands in Canada, @white2014direct also found that precipitation and clipping mediated species richness through shoot biomass, while warming had only direct negative effects. The direct decrease in Shannon diversity and species richness with warming in our study, was therefore likely caused by the loss of light demanding species (i.e. shift in the distribution of light affinity; @fig-toenails)(REFs?). Surprisingly, warming and increased biomass also shifted the communities towards moister conditions. Experimental warming by transplanting is often associated with a decrease in soil moisture because of higher evapotranspiration (REF). We found that soil moisture in the warmed sub-alpine communities was slightly higher compared to the ambient communities (Supplement Figure S1a), suggesting that the increased biomass captured soil moisture. This wetting effect was however not consistent across years, and might have been an exception for that year.

An alternative explanation for direct negative effect of nitrogen is soil acidification [@Kimmel2020-fo]. The distributions of reaction affinity shifted indeed strongly towards lower values indicating a community with more acidic conditions. Nitrogen addition decreased both diversity and evenness (Supplementary Figure S5), suggesting an increase in abundance of species that tolerate more acidic conditions. In our study, this explanation is also supported by an increase in available calcium at high levels of nitrogen addition, which can be released from the bedrock under acid conditions \[*we have data from PRS probes to show that*\].

### Clipping affects diversity indirectly, but grazing effects are much weaker

The effect of clipping on diversity was always mediated through community biomass. Interestingly, we found that clipping was able to prevent the loss of diversity and evenness under warming and nitrogen levels above 10 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^ at the alpine site (@fig-1-biomass-diversity b), suggesting this was related to competitive release [@Austrheim2001-nu; @klein2004experimental; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @post2023large]. Species loss was reduced at both clipping intensities, but only the intensive grazing treatment significantly increased diversity, suggesting that the medium grazing treatment was too low to effectively reduce competition for light in this community (i.e. less biomass reduction, @fig-1-biomass-diversity a). Clipping had no beneficial effect for biodiversity in the warmer and more productive sub-alpine community, despite reducing community biomass significantly, suggesting that the warmer sub-alpine community was too productive for our clipping treatments to effectively reduce competition.

The natural grazing treatment had similar but less effect on diversity compared to clipping. Although, grazing reduced community biomass similarly to clipping, the grazing had a weaker effect mediated through community biomass on diversity (and also on the other diversity indices). We used clipping treatments to mimic grazing, which might bias the results, however, the difference between cutting and grazing are often minimal [@talle2016grazing]. Since the overall grazing effects were similar compared to clipping, it suggests that our simulated grazing treatment is comparable to natural grazing and that additional effects of grazing, such as different timing of biomass removal, trampling, and fertilization from the animals did not override the effect of biomass removal per se.

Why weaker effect? Short-term study, other drivers are having negative effects (overriding grazing effect? additional species are available for colonisation...

**Some interesting points (unclear how to use these):**

-   Note that the warmed alpine and the unwarmed subalpine have very similar N slopes. They are living in the same climate! So even if the community is different, the N limitation is real at this temperature, but not colder (or warmer).

-   Biomass additive / compensatory effects of nitrogen and warming. The biomass of the warmed sub-alpine community did not increase above the maximum levels found at ambient climate, but reached the same biomass across the whole nitrogen gradient, indicating growth limited by other factors, possibly lower water availability at the warmer site(41), which might have been especially prominent due to a dry growing season in 2022 (Figure S1).

-   The major change in community biomass, diversity and evenness occurred at levels of nitrogen addition beyond 10 kg N ha\^-1\^ y^-1^, which is the critical load for significant changes in the structure and function of alpine and sub-alpine grasslands (35). This similar relationship between the warmed alpine and ambient sub-alpine communities suggests that colder alpine plant communities are not intrinsically less productive than those at lower elevation, but are limited by temperature-related environmental factors (27).

-   Interestingly, diversity indices based on change in abundance (i.e. evenness and diversity) showed more change in the cold alpine community in response to global change drivers, while indices based on change in species turnover (i.e. species richness and diversity), changed more in the warmer sub-alpine community. This might be because community changes in cold environments (i.e. the alpine) are often slow[(*45*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/ot2B) and changes in biomass (i.e. abundance) generally happen faster than species turnover (i.e. colonization or extinction) and there is often an extinction lag in alpine communities[(*14*, *15*, *46*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/ztDH+wbqE+5luD).

### Conclusions and implications

Our findings show that community biomass is a general indicator of mechanisms mediating global change impacts on plant diversity, in particular in colder and unproductive alpine grasslands. We found that several drivers including warming, nitrogen addition, clipping, and grazing work through the same mechanisms. However, at the same time, we also found that some drivers including warming and nitrogen addition operate through several mechanisms. \[*some implication, what does this mean: generally biomass works, but also direct effects are possible in particular in more productive systems?*\]. The relative importance of the drivers was not consistent across sites, advocates for replicating experiments across gradients and landscapes to allow more general understanding of ecological processes [@fraser2013coordinated; @prager2022integrating]. Our results showed that community proxies, such as environmental affinities can help to get a more general understanding of the underlying ecological processes.

\[*is this useful?*\] Our study was conducted over three years and thus looks at short-term responses, which can differ from long-term responses[(*56*, *57*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/egX7+3xXg). Long-term experiments across different climatic contexts are needed to understand where and how local adaptation of grazing regimes can be used as a tool to mitigate impacts of warming and pollution and inform adaptive management strategies that benefit biodiversity.
